entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Arius (c. 250 CE, Cyrenaica – 336 CE, Constantinople) was an influential Christian presbyter and theologian whose doctrines sparked the Arian Controversy, a profound schism that dominated the early Christian Church for over fifty years. Active primarily in Alexandria, Egypt, Arius challenged the nascent Trinitarian understanding of God, asserting the subordination of the Son (Jesus Christ) to God the Father. His teachings, which emphasized the Father's absolute transcendence and the Son's created nature, ignited fierce theological debates that compelled the Roman Emperor Constantine I to convene the First Council of Nicaea in 325 CE, a pivotal event in Christian history.

The core of Arius's theology, articulated around 318 CE, was the belief that 'there was a time when the Son was not' (ἦν ποτε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν). This assertion meant that the Son, while divine and pre-existent, was a created being, brought into existence by the Father out of nothing, and therefore not co-eternal or co-equal with the Father. Arius, then a presbyter in the Baucalis district of Alexandria, began publicly teaching these views, which were quickly condemned by his bishop, Alexander of Alexandria. The dispute escalated rapidly, drawing in other prominent bishops and theologians across the Eastern Roman Empire, including Eusebius of Nicomedia, who largely supported Arius, and Athanasius, who became Arius's staunchest opponent.
